page.description: Every year, browser vendors collaborate via the Interop project to synchronize their efforts on new HTML/CSS/JS features. page.text_excerpt: Skip to content Josh W Comeau Categories Courses Goodies About Search Disable sounds Activate dark mode RSS Feed The Future of CSS ✨ My top 10 picks for Interop 2027 Filed under CSS on October 20th, 2026 For the past few years, all of the major browser vendors (Google, Apple, Microsoft, and Mozilla, along with Igalia and Bocoup) have been working together on Interop (opens in new tab) , a project to improve universal browser support on web technologies. It’s been a remarkably successful effort; when a focus area gets added to Interop, it often winds up reaching near-100% support across all major browsers within a year. ✨ CSS Subgrid is a good example. Subgrid is a super-powerful extension to CSS Grid which enables entirely new layouts. It was implemented in Firefox back in 2019, but there wasn’t much movement with other browsers for years. They plan on using the ranking data to decide what to include for next year’s Interop! In this blog post, I want to dig into the top 10 features I voted for, to offer a bit of a preview of what CSS might look like within the next year. page.title: Good type against all odds – Unsung
page.description: A blog about software craft and quality
page.text_excerpt: SOFTWARE CRAFT AND QUALITY Search this site Results will appear as you type Clear HomeNewsletter + RSSAbout + ContactRandom post Good type against all odds This is not italics. This is not even oblique. This is a side effect of how those displays work. Instead of a whole rectangle of pixels being changed at once, the display is updated line by line, starting from the top one. As it’s moving towards the bottom, the internal horizontal position might have already advanced, the subsequent lines will be drawn slightly to the left, and it all leads to a slanted appearance. (This is in effect the same problem as rolling shutter in photography.) The interesting thing is that it could’ve gone the other way. Twice. In English or German, we treat scrolling left to be natural, and we consider only one direction of italic slant appropriate. The first has to do with the direction of reading. I believe the second is, like many things in typography, customary; there’s nothing inherently better than right-leaning letters, except we’re used to them since those are the only ones we ever see. But, the person putting it all together could’ve just as well done it the other way: scrolling to the right, or slanting to the left (by updating the display bottom to top – not as unusual as you might think!). Were those intentional choices, or was it a default? I’m not sure, but it points to the value of knowing this stuff, or creating a culture where this stuff is treasured. Often, more craft will require more work. Sometimes, however, you will get it for free – but only if you choose the right fork in the road. While we’re here, how about a few other examples of delightful moments in typography where I did not expect them? These, I believe, will be all intentional. But whether you consider them craft, or even good, I don’t know. page.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
page.description: Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it investigates its privacy.
page.text_excerpt: Skip to content ARS TECHNICA HOME SECTIONS FORUM SUBSCRIBE THEME SEARCH SIGN IN GHOSTSHARES Meta Muse exposes users’ personal and business secrets when they share conversations Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it investigates its privacy. DAN GOODIN – OCT 20, 2026 12:33 PM | 94 Credit: Getty Images Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that’s required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: a candidate’s notes preparing for a confidential executive-search call with a frontier AI lab, naming the lab’s internal contact and the meeting time a national marketing company’s internal revenue review, marked for its CEO a small-business owner’s loan application, with the amount requested a to-do list that included a bank fraud alert, with a partial account number

page.title: Academics have a duty to defend open knowledge systems like Wikipedia - LSE Impact
page.description: Wikipedia faces existential challenges from generative AI companies. Do researchers and teachers in higher education have an ethical duty to defend it?
page.text_excerpt: Politics Economics Business Technology Sustainability Society World Book Reviews Research Blogs Community Blogs LSE Impact Understanding impact and practice in academic research About Latest Submissions Follow Us Helen Choi October 19th, 2026 Academics have a duty to defend open knowledge systems like Wikipedia 0 comments | 6 shares Estimated reading time: 6 minutes 6 Shares Despite being the most widely consulted reference work ever created Wikipedia faces existential challenges from generative AI companies whose products divert traffic away from it. Helen Choi argues academics, by virtue of their responsibilities as researchers and teachers in higher education, have an ethical duty to defend and support open knowledge communities such as Wikipedia. When people use AI products like Google’s Gemini or ChatGPT, they are treated to immediate answers. Sometimes such answers include links to Wikipedia. However, most users of AI products do not click the links to Wikipedia, choosing instead to accept machine-generated outputs without further verification. If this practice continues, readership on Wikipedia will continue to decline. The AI threat to Wikipedia This is a problem for Wikipedia because it is run by a volunteer community that does everything from writing, coding, and administration, and this community comes from Wikipedia’s readers. A decline in the number of readers means fewer articles, updates, and corrections – and ultimately, a derelict and quite possibly defunct encyclopedia. This would be a loss for humanity as well as for the AI industry itself, as it is heavily reliant upon Wikipedia and its five billion words for training the systems that run their products. Wikipedia, of course, is more than training data for machines; it is a self-governing community of people that exists independently of commercial or governmental controls. A month before we released those results, a team from Citrini Research had approached us with an interesting question: could Claude (and AI drug discovery more generally) enable a group of motivated nonexperts to tackle a genuine problem in human health? page.title: Sixteen Years After Deepwater Horizon, Deep Sea Life Shows Few Signs of Recovery
page.text_excerpt: CLOSE / ← → Search SEARCH Yale Environment 360 Published at the Yale School of the Environment Explore Search About E360 E360 DIGEST OCTOBER 20, 2026 Sixteen Years After Deepwater Horizon, Deep Sea Life Shows Few Signs of Recovery An oil slick in the Gulf of Mexico after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010. KRIS KRÜG VIA WIKIPEDIA Sixteen years after an explosion on the Deepwater Horizon oil rig unleashed more than 4 million barrels of oil into the Gulf of Mexico, life in the deep sea has yet to recover. A new study finds that in the first few years after the 2010 disaster, populations of octopus, squid, krill, shrimp, and lanternfish declined by at least 60 percent. The research, based on acoustic surveys and thousands of netted samples across a broad swath of the Gulf of Mexico, found little evidence that life in the deep sea has bounced back. The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, described the losses as “the fastest and most severe” decline of animal life in the ocean layer that extends from about 600 feet deep to more than two miles down. While researchers stopped short of concluding that the oil spill had caused the declines, they said it was “the most parsimonious explanation.” Since the disaster, scientists have found oil-related compounds in the flesh of squid and octopus and in fish eggs deep underwater, contamination that they say can impair reproduction and development or lead to an early death. Lingering pollution may make it harder for deep-sea fish that are guided by their sense of smell to find mates. Beyond the drop in population numbers, the new study also found some declines in genetic diversity. The risk, authors say, is that populations may not harbor the genetic traits needed to survive in a rapidly changing world. Few workplace features are so scorned, yet seemingly so necessary. This paper provides the first large-scale economic evidence on workplace meetings using an original survey of more than 9,000 workers linked to matched employer–employee administrative data from Norway. We show that meetings are both common and costly, consuming an average of 12 percent of work hours and 14 percent of firm wage bills. Planning, problem solving, information sharing, and project coordination account for the majority of meeting activity. High-paying and high-revenue firms devote more resources to meetings despite facing a substantially higher opportunity cost of employee time. Meeting frequency and intensity are positively related to worker wage growth. Workers in meeting-intensive firms report greater on-the-job learning, and interactions with more senior colleagues are associated with stronger wage growth, suggesting that knowledge transmission within firms is an important mechanism. page.text_excerpt: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise 20th October 2026 The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores. How do we know? To demonstrate that the keys are compromised, the original reporter Wayne signed the following message with the private key of each of the eight intermediate CAs and reported it to the Root Program Teams on the 17th of October: We have a problem here - Wayne proof.zip contains the message, and for each intermediate the certificate, its public key and a signature on the message. To verify with OpenSSL: openssl x509 -in EM-DV-TLS-CA-G3B.crt.pem -noout -pubkey | diff - EM-DV-TLS-CA-G3B.pub.pem openssl dgst -sha384 -verify EM-DV-TLS-CA-G3B.pub.pem -signature EM-DV-TLS-CA-G3B.sig message.txt What actions have been taken? The root programs and many downstream trust stores have taken action to protect their users. The certificates have been blocked in Firefox and Chrome since the 17th of October, in Apple devices since the 19th and on Microsoft platforms since the 20th. The issue was responsibly disclosed to downstream trust stores on the 19th of October. Many have already released updates or are in the process of releasing updates. What are the consequences? An attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs could impersonate any website or service. This has already been remediated by Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple, and Chrome for their users through their tools for distributing revocation information such as OneCRL, CRLite and CRLSets. The CA has also revoked the compromised intermediate certificates. However, many other clients do not consume revocation information and require software updates to ensure they no longer trust the compromised intermediates. It also frees up a bunch of people with a fresh and deep understanding of the type system to work on new things. To give you a sense of scale, all of Tor has around 3000 exit relays, so roughly 10% were under their control. The attackers had gained access to the servers two months earlier, in August, and quietly deployed their Ebury 1.8.3 payload (an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer for Linux). The Attack The attack appears to have had two primary goals: Gather as much unencrypted mail traffic as possible Intercept SSH connections (MITM) By blocking certain ports, they made their exit nodes handle only unencrypted mail traffic. An interesting writeup by one of the victims (a veteran Tor operator) goes into great detail about that: lists.torproject.org/mailman3 In this post I'll focus on the second attack, the SSH MITM. If you happen to get a circuit that exits over one of those 333 infected exit nodes, you won't notice anything at first. Encrypted web traffic is forwarded as usual, but if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you're unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain. Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser. To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that. The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like. page.description: Hackers have published 281 GB of AfD emails as AI summaries, showing widespread antisemitism, racism, violent fantasies and alleged financial misconduct.
page.text_excerpt: HEIST News Features Food Map Interviews Weekend Podcast Sign in Subscribe News AfD AfD Leak: What 421,179 Hacked Emails Show about the German Far Right Hackers have published 281 GB of AfD emails as AI summaries, showing widespread antisemitism, racism, violent fantasies and alleged financial misconduct. HEIST · Tuesday, October 20, 2026 Share Image: Hexane.cc A vast archive of hacked emails from the AfD was published online on Monday: 281 GB containing 421,179 internal party emails. And, for anyone who might have grown confused about claims of antisemitism while it was plastered over the German news media in the weeks following the Berlin election: here you can see what it really looks like. In email after email, party supporters use racist slurs and share antisemitic theories of Jewish world domination; there are jokes about turning refugees into handbags and boots, discussions of whether refugees should be shot at the border, a Christmas card sent with a swastika and “Heil Hitler”, and an email thread signed off with “Heil und Sieg”. Sign in HEIST is a worker-owned online magazine, founded by writers and editors who after years working across Berlin's media landscape believed something essential was missing. Anyone living here has felt a growing gap between the city as it actually is and the version being served up by mainstream outlets. We experienced that disconnect firsthand. We saw political censorship shape coverage decisions and felt the weight of billionaire ownership land directly on our work. It reached a point where we could either keep going along with it, or try to build something better. That's why we created HEIST. page.text_excerpt: Skip to content Navigation Menu Platform Solutions Resources Open Source Enterprise Pricing Sign in Sign up microg GmsCore Repository navigation Code Issues 1.3k (1.3k) Pull requests 119 (119) Actions Wiki Security and quality 13 (13) Insights Home ale5000 edited this page · 23 revisions GmsCore Overview microG GmsCore is a free software reimplementation of Google's Play Services. It allows applications calling proprietary Google APIs to run on AOSP-based ROMs like LineageOS, acting as a free replacement for the non-free, proprietary Google Play Services (sometimes referred to as the more generic term "GApps"). It is a powerful tool to reclaim your privacy and freedom while enjoying Android core features (although apps you use that take advantage of it may still be using proprietary libraries to communicate with microG, just as they do when communicating with the actual Google Play Services). Features Opt-in to Google Services and extend application support On-/Offline location service Easy on battery, memory and CPU No bloatware Works on real devices, test emulators and virtual mobile infrastructure Free (open source) (Apache 2.0 licensed) System Requirements Your Android system needs to support signature spoofing so GmsCore can pretend the existence of the official Play Services to applications calling Google APIs. See the linked page to know about ROM providing out-of-the-box support and what you can do about the other ones. Modules GmsCore includes the Unified Network Location Provider module (UnifiedNlp) which handles application calls to Google's network location provider. For a full-working microG setup, you must also install a Play Store replacement application (like microG Companion). See installation. Project status The current status of implemented APIs is documented on this wiki page. Contributions welcome! page.title: Maxwell: The first Code Execution Model, by doubleAI
page.description: Maxwell improves code while it runs, adapting to hardware and data. Every improvement is formally proven equivalent to the original code.
page.text_excerpt: Maxwell Manifesto Research ↗ Get early access Maxwell : The first Code Execution Model by doubleAI Maxwell understands and improves code while it runs, reasoning about hardware and data, not just code. Every improvement is formally proven equivalent to the original code. Read the manifesto → Get early access 38× faster data processing pipelines 4.25× faster AI inference kernels What is a code execution model? This video didn’t load. Reload the page to try again. A short animated film, with narration and captions, introducing Maxwell: most code never sees the hardware it runs on or the data it processes. Maxwell watches a program while it runs, rewrites the binary underneath to fit that exact machine and data, and formally proves every improvement equivalent to the original. It runs on CPUs and GPUs, speeding up data pipelines and AI inference kernels. Featured customer LTX-2.5 generates 4K video in half the time LTX built LTX-2.5 for efficiency from day one, compiled end to end, sequence-parallel across GPUs, decoding on a hand-written attention kernel. A pipeline built and optimized by top human experts. Maxwell made their 4K generation nearly twice as fast. (opens ltx.io) This video didn’t load. Reload the page to try again. Each run is labelled in the video. The original pipeline takes 4 minutes 9 seconds; with Maxwell, the same clip takes 2 minutes 14 seconds.
